nameStory: The Rose Sun Star gets its charming name from its beautiful rose-pink to reddish coloration and its sunburst shape with multiple radiating arms. Like other sun stars, it has more arms than the typical five-armed starfish we usually picture, creating a spectacular sun-like appearance on the ocean floor.
description: The Rose Sun Star is a spectacular multi-armed sea star that looks like a living sunburst on the seafloor. Unlike the classic five-armed starfish, this beauty typically has 8-14 arms radiating from a central disc, creating an impressive star pattern. It displays gorgeous rose-pink to deep red colors, often with lighter bands or patterns across its arms. These sea stars can grow quite large, with arm spans reaching up to a foot across in mature specimens.

idTips.label: Multiple Arms
idTips.description: Count 8-14 arms radiating from the center, not the typical 5 arms of common starfish - this sunburst pattern is unmistakable

idTips.label: Rose-Pink Color
idTips.description: Beautiful rose-pink to deep red coloration, sometimes with lighter bands or mottled patterns across the arms

idTips.label: Rough Texture
idTips.description: Surface feels rough and bumpy to the touch, covered with small spines and granules that give it a sandpaper-like texture

idTips.label: Central Disc
idTips.description: Large, prominent central disc from which all arms radiate - the disc is noticeably thick and robust compared to the arms

idTips.label: Arm Shape
idTips.description: Arms are broad at the base and taper to rounded tips, not pointed like some starfish - they feel thick and substantial

habitat: Rose Sun Stars live in cold New England waters, typically found in deeper coastal areas from the low tide zone down to considerable depths. They prefer rocky bottoms, kelp beds, and areas with good water circulation where they can hunt for their preferred prey of other echinoderms and mollusks. You're most likely to spot them during very low tides in tide pools or while diving in rocky coastal areas, especially around places like the Maine coast or Cape Cod's deeper waters.

seasonality.spring: Best viewing season as warming waters may bring them into shallower areas. Look for them during extreme low tides in rocky tide pools.
seasonality.summer: Peak observation time for divers and snorkelers in deeper tide pools. Their rose-pink colors are most vibrant in the clearer summer waters.
seasonality.fall: Still active and visible, though they may start moving to slightly deeper waters. Fall storms can occasionally wash specimens ashore.
seasonality.winter: Rarely seen as they retreat to deeper, more stable waters. Any winter sightings are exceptional and usually involve specimens in very protected areas.

funFact: Rose Sun Stars are voracious predators that can actually push their stomach out of their body to digest prey externally - they'll wrap around a clam or mussel, pry it open with their powerful arms, then slip their stomach inside the shell to dissolve and absorb their meal!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other multi-armed starfish, but the Rose Sun Star's distinctive rose-pink color and 8+ arms make it fairly unique. Remember: if it's pink and has more arms than you can count on one hand, you've probably found a Rose Sun Star!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'starfish,' Rose Sun Stars aren't fish at all - they're echinoderms, more closely related to sea urchins and sand dollars. The name 'sea star' is more accurate, which is why marine biologists prefer that term.
compareHints: The Rose Sun Star is the only Crossaster species in New England waters, making identification easier once you know the multi-armed sunburst pattern. It differs from other sun star family members by its distinctive rose-pink coloration and typically having more arms (8-14) than most related species. Other multi-armed starfish in the region tend to be different colors or have fewer arms.
